title: Best Of Enemies - review
transcript: best of enemies at the young vic is the best new play i've seen this year james graham's writing is vivid funny shocking the acting by the two leads david harwood and charles edwards is electrifying and the production directed by jeremy herring with a set by bunny christie is perfect and i'm saying all this up front before anything else because when i tell you what it's about there's a big danger you'll skip to the next video and i really don't want you to because this is great theater that deserves to be seen and there will be opportunities for you to see it streaming if you can't get to the young vic best of enemies tells you a lot about the polarized society we live in today that's true but it's also just simple gripping entertainment i'm paul seven lewis this is one minute theater reviews and i'm reviewing best of enemies at the young vic in a co-production with headlong well you've had a minute but keep watching and i'll tell you a lot more about why i give it five stars so why might you think best of enemies is not for you well because it's about the 1968 presidential election and in particular some televised debates between the influential conservative thinker william f buckley and the liberal writer gore vidal i know it sounds boring but believe me it's not james graham's play begins with the immediate aftermath of one of the debates there's anger and shock at language that has been used although at that point we don't know what's been said or how it's come to this so we then go back and see that the story began with abc tv news desperate to chase some ratings deciding to have well-known intellectuals talking about the presidential conventions at which the republican democratic candidates are elected and this was the first time this had happened so the play is partly about the corrupting influence of tv and there are three big video screens high up at the back of the stage which also shows us the studio control area we see how the participants both take part because they see it as a way of promoting themselves and thinking not a lot beyond that we then see over a series of debates how the confrontational format generated more heat than light and we see that how they come across is more important than what they say buckley's wife pat says at one point that's all this is who do i like the most and at the end vidal prophesies that this means that one day a candidate could get elected because he was more likeable rather than having the best policies and don't we know it okay that's the bones of it but what james graham has done is flesh that skeleton with bits of verbatim speech from the debates and lots of fictional dialogue behind from behind the scenes that brings to life the two protagonists well they're both intellectuals and they're both narcissists they really want to win the debate so that i guess they can be more influential in the world of politics and each of them is delighted when they're recognized by leading politicians and the two leads charge the production with electricity david harewood plays william f buckley now you might be surprised that a black actor is playing a right winger whose whiteness was part of who he was but a good actor inhabits the role and in this case the role is of a man not comfortable in his own skin mr harwood relishes the part not only the external mannerisms ticks and lip licking and other nervous signs but also the inner person his sincerity and the source of his beliefs the the devoted husband the outsider and the desperation to win mr hayward does a remarkable job of making us feel sympathy for someone who could so easily be the villain because of his racism and homophobia and when the first debates go badly for him under an onslaught from vidal i actually felt sorry for him but then you see him planning to raise his game charles edwards conveys the smooth charm the rays of wit the obsession with power and the vulnerability of vidal he was a patrician and his sense of superiority while insufferable helps him dominate those early debates but then buckley starts to score points and as vidal squirms so do we but they live in ivory towers not what most of the electorate would recognize as the real world i mean they're not portrayed as bad people their extreme views seem to be more like an academic exercise than something from the heart but they do have hearts and it's their pride above all this desire to win that drives them from civilized conversation to conflict to playground name calling both seek out each other's weaknesses initially of their arguments but eventually personal ones and you find yourself not wanting to look as their feelings are exposed obsessed by their personal dislike of each other they don't even anticipate the effect of their clashes on the world of politics which is moving from compromise to polarization in the real world things fall apart we're shown something of what's going on in that real world or at least the demonstration so 1968 was already a significant year robert kennedy and martin luther king were assassinated uh an extremist shot anti-what andy warhol there were protests about the vietnam war but when we look back we see that this was the beginning of the end of consensus and the start of polarization left versus right young versus old plus conflicts of gender race sexuality and on the other hand the so-called silent majority which presidential candidate richard nixon appealed to so tempers are rising creating a sense of a pressure cooker the set itself by bunny christie is a small open stage surrounded on three sides by audience turning the protagonists into gladiators in an arena the other actors also light up the stage i'll pick out claire foster as buckley's cheerful wife patricia cyrus lowe lowers the drawing but angry and incisive james baldwin and john hodgkinson who plays the chair of the debates reveling in the viewing figures but out of control of the wild horse he's set off riding it's only a cast of ten but they take on many characters all well delineated so you might think there are twice as many in the cast and it seems like every one of the characters has a contribution to make and every line seems to have something to say under the direction of james herron this production zinged along and as with the wolf hall trilogy or james graham's this house which he also directed he uses movement to add physical excitement to the dialogue i mean i like the way he and james graham make politics exciting because politicians shape our country and it's a crying shame we find them boring or see them reduced to personality and why were they the best of enemies well they needed one another and they're really quite similar so five stars and please see it preferably at the young vic but if that's not possible well they promise that there'll be some performances streamed i hope you found this review worth watching if you want to be the first to know about my future reviews please subscribe to one minute theater reviews using the button below you can also read my reviews on the website one minute theater reviews dot co dot uk and you'll also find me posting as one minute theater reviews on instagram facebook and twitter thank you for watching
